references.text: Jesus also eats at a Pharisee's house on another occasion: [ref:Luk 7:36|Luke 7:36]. The Pharisees invited Jesus to meals, which repeatedly provided opportunities for confrontations and teaching.
Once again, Jesus is invited to eat at a Pharisee's house in [ref:Luk 11:37|Luke 11:37], showing a pattern where the Pharisees observe Jesus during meals.

The Pharisees and scribes kept watch on Jesus to find something to accuse him of, especially concerning the Sabbath, as described in [ref:Luk 6:7|Luke 6:7]. The expression "παρατηρούμενοι" (keeping watch) is also used there.
In [ref:Luk 20:20|Luke 20:20], opponents keep Jesus under surveillance (παρατηρήσαντες) to catch him in his words. This shows the same motive of monitoring and hostile observation.
In [ref:Mark 3:2|Mark 3:2], they watch Jesus on the Sabbath to see if he will heal, just as the Pharisees observe him here.
The Sabbath controversy in [ref:Luk 13:14|Luke 13:14], where the synagogue leader reacts to Jesus healing on the Sabbath, forms a close context for the Sabbath healing that follows in Luke 14.
The following passage [ref:Luk 14:2-6|Luke 14:2–6] shows exactly what the Pharisees were watching for—Jesus heals a man with dropsy on the Sabbath and defends his action.
In [ref:Matt 12:10|Matthew 12:10], the Pharisees ask Jesus if it is lawful to heal on the Sabbath, again with the intent of finding grounds to accuse him.
[ref:Sal 37:32|Psalm 37:32] describes the wicked lying in wait for the righteous and seeking to take his life, a motive reflected in the Pharisees' surveillance of Jesus.
In [ref:Jer 20:10|Jeremiah 20:10], the prophet speaks of people who lie in wait for him and wait for him to fall, which recalls the hostile observation Jesus faced.
